item.title: UK drought highlights precarious food system
item.description: Farmers are reporting dry soil and poor crop conditions while the country’s fresh produce depends on increasingly uncertain global supplies.
item.content:encoded:
Much of England is now officially in drought. Reservoir levels are being closely monitored by water companies, while farmers are reporting dry soils and poor crop conditions. Further restrictions such as grazing rules could soon come into effect.

Water is recognised as critical national infrastructure. However, drought does not only threaten our water supply. It also tests the resilience of the food system that depends on it.

For most of us, that reality becomes visible in the supermarket: standing in front of a shelf with no cucumbers, more expensive tomatoes or fewer fresh vegetables to choose from. These episodes have become increasingly familiar in recent years. We notice the empty shelves, accept the higher prices and move on.

But I keep wondering: why does this surprise so many people?

The UK carefully monitors many of the systems that underpin everyday life. We publish inflation figures every month, NHS waiting lists every week and regularly report on water reservoir levels because these indicators tell us whether essential systems are becoming stronger or weaker. They provide an early indication that intervention may be needed before problems escalate. Food, however, is different. We tend to judge the resilience of our food system only after something has gone wrong.

That seems odd for something so fundamental. Food is every bit as essential as healthcare, energy or water,...

item.title: ‘Sophie, Standing There’: After ‘Sorrow and Bliss’, Meg Mason’s new novel asks if books can save us
item.description: Author Meg Mason palpates the tender spots that linger in the wake of divorce, infertility, long-term job insecurity and even the wounds religion may inflict.
item.content:encoded:
I sometimes say that My Family and Other Animals – Gerald Durrell’s autobiographical novel from 1956 – saved my life. My mother pressed her dog-eared copy into my hands during a year I was hospitalised repeatedly for major depression.

The sun-soaked Greek island of Corfu – as well as the Durrell family’s foibles and adventures – felt a world away from my hometown’s bleak winter and all those blister packets and doctors’ waiting rooms. I became fascinated by Durrell’s colourful childhood and his longstanding career as both an author and a naturalist. I could easily recall the story’s funniest moments and parrot the most memorable lines.

On even the hardest days, it somehow seemed to help.

This may seem like a roundabout way of introducing Sophie, Standing There, the new novel by New Zealand–born, Sydney-based Meg Mason, which centres on a soon-to-be-divorced festival worker and her fixation on an author whose work begins to speak to her. But this story, too, is about what books and authors can mean to us at particular times, and how they might save us – sometimes not only in their what but also in their when.

item.title: Rare Eurasian lynx recorded on camera traps in Sikkim
item.description: The image was captured in Tso Lhamo, a high-altitude border landscape.
item.content:encoded:
A Eurasian lynx has been recorded in a camera-trap image from the Tso Lhamo plateau in Sikkim. This encounter marks the first confirmed photographic evidence of the species in the state. It is also the second such record from the Eastern Himalayas. The image, captured in January 2026 at an altitude of 5,250 metres in Mangan district, shows the animal moving across a rocky, sparsely vegetated high-altitude slope.

The sighting comes from a long-term snow leopard and rangeland monitoring programme led by the Sikkim forest department and WWF-India. The initiative tracks snow leopards and associated wildlife while studying the ecological condition of the trans-Himalayan rangelands.

The Sikkim record follows a 2025 photographic documentation of a Eurasian lynx in Arunachal Pradesh during a joint survey by WWF-India and the Arunachal Pradesh forest department.

“It highlights the ecological significance of our high-altitude rangelands and reinforces our commitment to protecting these fragile ecosystems. The cooperation of the Lachen Dzumsa (traditional local self-governance body) in facilitating access to these remote areas has been important to this work,” Sikkim’s Chief Conservator of Forests (Wildlife), Udai Gurung, said in a press note.

item.title: Indonesia: At least 38 dead as 7.7-magnitude earthquake strikes eastern coast
item.description: Tsunami waves of less than 3 feet were recorded in several regions after the tremors, but an official warning was lifted three hours after the quake.
item.content:encoded:
A 7.7 magnitude earthquake struck eastern Indonesia early on Saturday, killing at least 38 and injuring over a dozen residents, AP reported.

The earthquake hit Indonesia’s Flores region at a depth of 10 kilometres at 5.58 am local time, the news agency quoted the United States Geological Survey as saying. The epicentre of the quake was located 68 kilometres northwest of the city of Ende.

After the earthquake, tsunami waves of less than 3 feet were recorded in several parts of Indonesia, Reuters reported. The tsunami warning was lifted three hours after the quake.

“As of 15:00 [0800 GMT], the recorded figures are 38 fatalities, two people seriously injured, 11 with minor injuries,” Suharyanto, head of the ​National Disaster Management Agency, was quoted by Reuters as having said at a press conference. About 2,000 people had fled to safer ground, he said.

Sixteen bodies were pulled out from the site of a landslide in the village of Reok in the Manggarai region.

Strong tremors were also felt in the regions of East Nusa Tenggara, West ​Nusa Tenggara and parts of ⁠South Sulawesi. In many places, residents reported shaking that lasted about a minute, Reuters reported.

item.title: Centre cuts windfall tax on petrol, diesel and aviation fuel
item.description: The special duty on diesel exports has been cut to Rs 24 from Rs 25.5, on aviation fuel to Rs 19.5 from Rs 22 and on petrol to zero from Rs 3.5.
item.content:encoded:
The Union Finance Ministry has cut the windfall tax on exports of petrol, diesel and aviation turbine fuel from Saturday, according to a gazette notification.

India first imposed the windfall tax in July 2022 to capture extraordinary gains made by oil companies as crude prices surged. The tax was scrapped two years later and reintroduced in March after oil prices rose amid the crisis in West Asia.

The special additional excise duty, through which the windfall tax is levied, has been cut on diesel exports to Rs 24 per litre from Rs 25.5.

The duty on aviation turbine fuel exports has been reduced to Rs 19.5 per litre from Rs 22, while the levy on petrol exports has been cut to zero from Rs 3.5 per litre.

The revised rates took effect on Saturday. There was no change in the existing duty rates on petrol and diesel sold for domestic consumption.

The government imposed the export duty on diesel and aviation turbine fuel on March 27 and has revised the rates every fortnight. The levy was extended to petrol exports from May 16.

The windfall tax is intended to ensure domestic availability of petroleum products and discourage exporters from benefiting excessively from differences between domestic and international prices.

Triage, Claudia Rankine

Two friends meet in an art gallery after decades of silence. The idealism that once bound them together fissured and fractured under the weight of collective and personal griefs. Through their memories of youthful certainty, the antagonism of their conversation and the embers of their enduring kinship, they navigate the wreckage of our world today – the hope, the anger and the exhaustion.

In 2024, Nina’s small aircraft crashes into a lake in the Wyoming mountains. Lost, freezing and alone, she stumbles upon Sunrise – an abandoned frontier town that is strangely well-maintained.

In 2003, Sunrise’s golden boy Coll is about to start rehearsals for the town's annual historical reenactment when he is linked with a scandalous incident at a local bar. item.title: ‘Appetite’: Life in Goa comes alive in this wryly humorous yet eerily chilling anthology
item.description: Edited by Shivranjana Rathore and Tino De Sa, it has short stories, poems, essays, memoir pieces, and a graphic narrative exploring Goa’s various sides.
item.content:encoded:
It is difficult to not romanticise Goa. Not the hyper-curated, exaggeratedly aestheticised party destination that lives in perpetual revelry on Instagram, or the casino capital that flashy billboards at the Dabolim airport promise, but the real deal. Small villages that awaken at daybreak. Old Portuguese houses with their red benches, often under the strict surveillance of a resident dog or two. The sound of the poder and the satisfaction of biting into the still-warm crust of a fresh poi. The energy of Mapusa market. The seven hundred and sixty-five distinct shades of green that form the landscape of monsoon months. The roiling July sea that humbles the most intrepid of tourists and adventurers. The inviting plates of ambotik and xacuti, and the sticky sweetness of dodol.

All this, if you are an outsider looking in. More, if you claim kinship with the land, the history, the culture. It is this liminality between longing and belonging that Shivranjana Rathore and Tino De Sa’s anthology of new writing from Goa captures.

item.title: Post July uprising, Bangladesh has rediscovered 1947 – but forgotten those uprooted by Partition
item.description: The events of 1947 are increasingly being revived as a way of reasserting Bengali Muslim political identity and creating distance from India.
item.content:encoded:
For years, August 15 in Bangladesh commemorated one event above all others: the assassination of the country’s founding president, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, and most of his family in 1975. It was observed as a day of state mourning.

It rarely evoked the day British rule over the subcontinent ended in 1947 and Bengal was bifurcated. That older date was treated as an event belonging only to India and Pakistan (which attained independence one day earlier).

Bangladesh, after all, was a nation born only in 1971, the “east wing” of Pakistan that achieved its independence after a bloody Liberation War.

But now, two years after the July uprising that brought down Sheikh Hasina’s government and turned her father Sheikh Mujib into a taboo subject, that quiet estrangement from 1947 shows signs of ending.

However, the reasons for this deserve as much scrutiny as the shift itself.

An awkward question

Bangladesh’s reluctance to dwell on Partition was never simply a matter of forgetting. It reflected a deeper discomfort about where 1947 belonged in a national story built overwhelmingly around 1971.

To examine the creation of Pakistan honestly is to ask whether the Two-Nation Theory – the idea that the subcontinent’s Hindus and Muslims constituted separate nations – was sound in the first place.

item.title: ‘The Once and Future Riot’: Graphic journalism in the post-truth era that shows the truth isn’t neat
item.description: The book’s central contention is that sectarian violence in modern India is not an isolated, anomalous incident, but a recurring structural mechanism.
item.content:encoded:
The title of Joe Sacco’s latest graphic narrative, The Once and Future Riot, is unlike Palestine, Footnotes in Gaza, or The Fixer. Not immediately referencing a place or a people, The Once and Future Riot indicates a sense of tension instead. And not just between past, present and future, but also palpably in the ability of the journalist or the graphic artist to draw their reader towards some semblance of “truth”.

Throughout his career, Sacco has been well aware of the complexity of bearing or collecting witness, including the ethical complications and subject unreliability. He knows objective facts carry less weight in shaping public opinion than appeals to emotion, personal belief and pre-existing worldviews. However, Sacco finds himself on even shakier ground here, represented in the densely populated, chaotic page architecture of this narrative. His usual immersive research process of relying on the use of multiple eyewitness testimonies combined with including himself as a character in the narrative proves to be not enough.

The National Human Rights Commission on Friday said that it had issued notice to the Union government following reports that 19 Central Reserve Police Force personnel died allegedly by suicide between January and May 22, PTI reported.

The rights panel said that the reported figures raise concern about the well-being and safety of the paramilitary force personnel.

Taking suo moto cognisance of an August 11 news report, the panel noted that 59 personnel reportedly died by suicide in 2025, the highest number recorded by the force in the last five years.

The commission has issued notices to the Union Home Secretary and the force’s director general, seeking a detailed report within two weeks.

According to the media report, 281 Central Reserve Police Force personnel died by suicide in the last five years, of whom 216 were on duty. The force recorded 57 suicides in 2021, 43 in 2022, 57 in 2023 and 46 in 2024, the rights panel noted.

item.title: History remembered: When Pakistan wanted to fly its flag at London’s India House on August 15, 1947
item.description: Britain announced its exit from India nearly a year ahead of schedule, leaving many loose ends to be tied up before the first Independence Day.
item.content:encoded:
As August 1947 drew near, MK Vellodi was faced with a peculiar problem. The seasoned civil servant from Madras had taken over as the acting High Commissioner of British India to the UK only a few months before, in April. He had been tasked with overseeing the Independence Day celebrations at the historic India House, British India’s diplomatic mission in London, on August 15.

But, as he explained in a telegram to the Ministry of External Affairs and Commonwealth Relations in New Delhi on July 22, he had still not received proper instructions from the government of India about the event. He needed them sent well in time so that he could make the necessary arrangements.

Vellodi also complained that the mission had no national flag to hoist, so he would need details of the colours and dimensions of the tricolour.

The lack of such details isn’t surprising. Lord Mountbatten, the British viceroy, had announced only on June 3 that the colonial power would leave India on August 15, instead of the earlier scheduled date of June 30, 1948. He also declared that British India would be divided into India and Pakistan.

item.title: Saudi defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan is a verdict on American reliability
item.description: It’s an insurance policy taken out by governments that no longer wish to entrust their safety to a single guarantor.
item.content:encoded:
Commentators predictably reacted to the news of the signing of a mutual defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on August 7 by reaching for the label “Islamic Nato”. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement stipulates that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all. Jerusalem went a step further, describing the alliance as an anti-Israel alliance.

But the Nato comparison is the wrong framing. Three of America’s own partners have bound themselves together – and the most consequential audience for what they signed sits not in Tehran or Tel Aviv but in Washington. The agreement reads, in effect, as a verdict on American reliability.

On paper, the combination is formidable. Turkey fields Nato’s second-largest army and a drone industry that has reshaped modern battlefields. Saudi Arabia brings the Gulf’s deepest reserves of capital. Pakistan adds a large, combat-experienced military and the Muslim world’s only nuclear arsenal. Analysts point to genuinely complementary assets here: Turkish technology which is short of markets, Pakistani manpower short of financing, Saudi wealth short of manpower.

This pact did not appear from nowhere. It extends a Saudi-Pakistani agreement of September 2025, signed days after Israel’s strike on Hamas targets in Doha, Qatar, and was made more urgent by the US-Israeli war...

item.title: In Bangladesh, jute mandate can’t stop switch to plastic sacks
item.description: Synthetic fibres have made inroads due to easy availability and low cost.
item.content:encoded:
Bangladesh is the world’s second largest producer of the environmentally friendly fiber jute. However, the country has, for decades, grappled with the move to combat the escalating use of the cheaper and more popular, but harmful, plastic-based packaging and synthetic fibers.

As a safeguard measure, the government, 16 years ago, enacted a law for the mandatory use of jute sacks and bags to contain and carry 19 essential commodities, including rice, wheat and fertiliser.

The move has been largely unsuccessful, though, with plastic and synthetic fiber invasion as packaging ingredients continuing unabated. Synthetic and poly bags have caused environmental problems such as waste disposal.

Nazmul Haque, the government-appointed jute officer in the northern Sherpur district, told Mongabay that a small semi-automatic rice mill – Sakhina Rice Mill – has exclusively been using jute sacks.

item.content:encoded:
Two Naga persons were killed in firing by suspected militants in Manipur’s Kangpokpi district on Friday, Ukhrul Times reported.

A group of men armed with “sophisticated weapons” attacked Langka Naga village at around 8 am, an unidentified police officer told PTI.

The officer said that a man identified as W Chawang died at the scene after suffering gunshot wounds to the head, while three others were injured.

The second person who died has been identified as Kawidinang Abonmai, India Today NE reported.

Residents said that an armed group from the Naga village also opened fire at the suspected attackers following the incident, PTI reported.

The Liangmai Naga Council-Manipur condemned the attack and alleged that militants from the Kuki National Front (P) were behind it.

The council announced an immediate total shutdown of Liangmai Naga-inhabited areas of Manipur until further notice.

It said shops, officers institutions and non-essential activities would remain closed, while medical, fire and other emergency services would be exempted.

It also appealed to residents to remain calm and urged the authorities to ensure public safety and bring those responsible to justice.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Days with My Red-Flag Girlfriend’, by Kajol Aikat.
item.content:encoded:
Every good love story includes a Holi celebration.

But personally, I never felt the festival was romantic in any conventional sense. It’s loud, anarchic and someone always gets colour in their mouth. The thandai is spiked by someone who doesn’t announce it. The white clothes you wore, ironically, are destroyed within four minutes. Someone’s playlist is terrible. Someone’s playlist is perfect. It doesn’t matter. But maybe that’s the point.

Holi felt better that year.

The festivities happened on the college lawn, which had been transformed overnight into something between a fever dream and a Bollywood set that had run out of budget but not enthusiasm. There was colour everywhere – powder smeared on the walls, footprints of pink and green tracking across the concrete, clouds of dry gulal drifting through the air like slow, festive smoke. Some guy from the third floor had dragged a JBL speaker the size of a small refrigerator down four flights of stairs purely for this moment, and it was playing “Genda Phool” at a volume that suggested he felt the song had never been heard at its true potential before.

item.title: Tata Group Chairman N Chandrasekaran has resigned. How did the group start its ‘swadeshi’ business?
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Tata: The Global Corporation That Built Indian Capitalism’, by Mircea Raianu.
item.content:encoded:
Early in 1864, a young Parsi merchant from Bombay named Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata set sail for ­ England, carry­ing a set of bills of exchange backed by a consignment of Indian cotton. By the time the ship docked in Liverpool, the price of cotton had fallen so quickly that the bills became worthless. Un- expectedly forced to manage the liquidation of his ­ father’s firm, Jamsetji took time to observe the workings of the textile mills in Lancashire, the heartland of the Industrial Revolution. When he returned to India a few months ­ later, he found Bombay in the grip of a disastrous financial crisis. The ­ whole of the city, Jamsetji’s first biographer ­ later recalled, “was sitting on the stool of repentance, with sackcloth and ashes; while the disconsolate creditors held Dharma at the door of their ruined debtors.” Out of this chastening experience arose India’s own Industrial Revolution, more modest and ­ limited in scope than its British counterpart but all the more impressive for the constraints it had to overcome.

item.description: Rajkumar Santoshi’s adaptation of the play ‘Jis Lahore Nai Vekhya, O Jamya E Nai’ is out in cinemas.
item.content:encoded:
A chunk of Sunny Deol’s career is devoted to swinging hand pumps at Pakistanis, bashing in their heads or simply bellowing at them until their eardrums burst. In Rajkumar Santoshi’s Batwara 1947, Deol is in a different zone and a different register.

The Hindi-Punjabi film is adapted from a play about compassion trumping communal hatred during the horrific time of Partition. Even Sunny Deol, then, must behave.

Deol plays Sikandar, a Muslim businessman from Meerut who flees to Lahore after being targetted by Hindu rioters. Sikandar, his wife Hamida (Preity Zinta) and daughter Tanno (Khushi Hajare) enter the mansion allotted to them, only to find an elderly Hindu woman there.

The house belongs to Durgavati (Shabana Azmi). Her own son and his family are missing. Durgavati refuses to leave until her son returns.

The domestic quandary is soon eclipsed by the antics of the fanatic politician Yaqub (Abhimanyu Singh), who wants to purge the neighbourhood of its Hindu past. item.title: Census 2027: Caste, Covid-19 vaccination status among 40 questions notified by Centre
item.description: This will be the first time in independent India that caste will be enumerated across communities.
item.content:encoded:
The Census 2027 will ask respondents if they belong to a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, and will also include an open-ended question for other communities about the caste that they belong to.

This will be the first time in independent India that caste will be enumerated across communities. Until now, Census exercises only recorded the population of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

Among the 40 questions notified on Friday are also those seeking information on the place where respondents received their Covid-19 vaccination, the total number of bank accounts they hold and digital literacy. The form also seeks information on Aadhaar numbers, mobile numbers, passport numbers and voter IDs.

The population enumeration phase of the census will take place from September 1 to September 30 in Ladakh and snow-bound non-synchronous areas of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, according to a gazette notification issued earlier this month. The online self-enumeration window for the second phase will be open from August 17 to August 31.

It will be conducted in other parts of the country in February 2027.

The Comptroller and Auditor General has flagged that the forest cover increased by only 0.03 million hectares against a target of 1.4 million hectares in the last 10 years under the Green India Mission, reported The Times of India on Thursday. This is a shortfall of 97.5% from the target.

Launched in February 2014, the Green India Mission is an initiative under the National Action Plan on Climate Change to protect, restore, and enhance the forest cover of India.

The audit report tabled in Parliament on Wednesday said that the shortfall in implementing the mission was due to poor financial planning and non-alignment with existing state and central schemes, reported Hindustan Times.

There was also a lack of monitoring of the interventions made under the mission, according to The Times of India.

The report covered interventions made under the mission in 16 states and Union territories for which financial targets between the financial years 2015-’16 and 2024-’25 were approved by the Ministry of Environment.

The Rajasthan Cabinet on Thursday approved a bill on Uniform Civil Code to ban polygamy and make the registration of marriages and divorces mandatory within 60 days, The Hindu reported.

The bill, approved ahead of the imposition of the model code of conduct for the upcoming panchayat and local body elections, will be introduced in the Assembly during its monsoon session beginning on August 20

Rajasthan is the fifth Bharatiya Janata Party-ruled state to move towards implementing a common personal law framework.

The Uniform Civil Code aims to introduce a common set of laws governing marriage, divorce, succession and adoption for all citizens. Currently, such personal affairs of different religions are based on community-specific laws, largely derived from religious scripture.

The Rajasthan bill has proposed provisions to establish equal property rights for sons and daughters across religions, irrespective of their personal laws, reported The Hindu.

The bill also proposes mandatory registration or written intimation of the beginning and end of live-in relationships.

The Uniform Civil Code would not apply to Scheduled Tribes and communities whose customary rights are protected under the Constitution, the newspaper quoted minister Jogaram Patel as saying.

item.title: In Pakistan, Prisoner No 804 seems to be everywhere
item.description: By jailing former Prime Minister Imran Khan, the country’s establishment aimed to doom him to irrelevance. But he has rendered him more relevant than ever.
item.content:encoded:
It wasn’t unlike a solitary vigil.

On August 1, a social media post appeared showing a woman standing outside the Karachi Press Club, holding a painted portrait of Imran Khan, bearing the words: “Imran Khan ko riha karo”, free Imran Khan, and “Hamara leader hamen wapas dedo”, give our leader back to us.

The image of her quiet defiance elided with the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf’s reignited street mobilisation, marking their leader’s three-year anniversary in prison.

Together, these instances illuminate a peculiar paradox: three years of incarceration instead of diminishing the former Pakistani prime minister’s symbolic appeal seem to actually have bolstered it.

Pakistan’s political playbook has long been recycled. Something drives a wedge between a political leader and the establishment. What follows is familiar: some combination of dismissal, disqualification, imprisonment or exile, with the eventual aim of irrelevance. Once enough time has passed and the political storm settles, an accommodation is usually reached.

The case of Khan somewhat unsettled the playbook. Khan’s own ascent to power was hardly predictable. Cricketing fame was followed by philanthropy and eventually politics, despite his initial reluctance to enter the field. item.title: What is Gen Z’s dark and nonsensical humor trying to say?
item.description: It is less about moral values but the product of a desire to engage in more authentic conversations about what they believe.
item.content:encoded:
After Luigi Mangione was arrested in December 2024 in connection with the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, the internet did what it often does: It turned something serious into a joke.

Although Mangione has pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder in New York and to federal stalking charges, viral memes at the time romanticised him as a popular – and incredibly attractive – man of the people who made corporate elites within the American health insurance industry afraid.

Some of these memes adhered to conventional forms of political satire. One, for example, quoted a speech from the movie A Bug’s Life in which a villainous grasshopper argues for the need to punish the movie’s ant protagonist to keep the other ants in line. In this meme, the political point was clear: Elites preserve power by making examples of insignificant ants who dare to challenge them.

The point was less clear with other memes, including celebrations of Mangione’s fashion-forward shackled ankles in court and mock Burger King advertisements referencing the fact that a McDonald’s employee had been the one to call law enforcement on him: “Burger King: We won’t turn you in to the Feds.” Rather than being ironic, they are unserious.

item.title: Sugarcane powers India’s rural economy but climate change is affecting yield
item.description: The crop sustains millions of farmers but concerns are growing over its water demands as the changing weather poses challenges.
item.content:encoded:
Sugarcane cultivation across parts of India’s Deccan Plateau is becoming more productive. But, it is also becoming more vulnerable to climate variability, a new long-term study finds.

Sugarcane has long shaped India’s rural economy. It powers sugar mills, supports ethanol and bioenergy production, and sustains millions of farmers. But the crop is also at the centre of mounting concerns over water use, particularly in semi-arid regions facing recurrent droughts and groundwater stress.

The study analysed 22 years of sugarcane production trends across five districts in Maharashtra and Karnataka to understand how cultivation, yields and production patterns have changed under varying climatic conditions.

“We noticed that sugarcane cultivation in Maharashtra and Karnataka was increasingly being affected by climatic variability, even though it remains one of the most important economic activities across the Deccan Plateau,” says Krishna Kumar from the Department of Applied Science and Humanities at MIT-ADT University, Pune, and one of the study’s researchers.

Across climate zones

Sugarcane production trends in India have been studied extensively at national and state levels, but long-term district-level analyses incorporating weather variability remain limited.

item.title: Nisha da Cunha (1934-2026): An inspirational teacher and writer of things usually left unsaid
item.description: Her literary contribution is particularly significant for its topicality today, writes a former student.

Some people come to us to definitively shape who we later become. Call it providence, fate, destiny, chance or sheer good luck, but Professor Nisha da Cunha, who died on August 11, was one such provocateur in my life.

My recollections of her are perhaps common to every student of English Literature at St Xavier's College of the mid- and late 1970s – the commanding air, the measured diction while reading a text aloud in the classroom, trademark poise, impatience with students who "showed off" and her passionate guidance of those she believed had potential.

It is not an exaggeration to say that we not only wanted to be as bright as she was, we actually wanted to be her, down to her short hair, piercing gaze, woven saree and large red bindi. item.title: What happened to Modi’s $5 trillion economy promise?
item.description: The India Fix: A newsletter on Indian politics from Scroll.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The India Fix by Shoaib Daniyal. A newsletter on Indian politics.

As always, if you’ve been sent this newsletter and like it, to get it in your inbox every week, sign up here (click on “follow”).

Las week, Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced in Parliament that India’s gross domestic product would hit the $5 trillion mark in 2029.

It’s a banal projection predicated on the simple maths of compounding. The Indian economy, valued at nearly $4 trillion, is growing so it will inevitably touch that mark one day. item.title: What decolonising economics can look like
item.description: The discipline has largely overlooked how colonialism, empire and unequal power have shaped economic development.
item.content:encoded:
Economics shapes many aspects of our daily lives, from the prices we pay to the policies governments adopt. Yet many of the ideas taught as universal principles of economics emerged from a narrow historical context and have rarely been examined through a decolonial lens.

A recently published book, Decolonizing Economics, argues that economics is long overdue for decolonisation. Its authors contend that the discipline has largely overlooked how colonialism, empire and unequal power shaped the development of modern economies and the economic theories used to explain them.

Decolonising economics means rethinking how we understand economic development and inequality. Rather than explaining prosperity through technology, markets and scientific progress, it examines how colonisation, resource extraction and exploited labour shaped today’s wealthy economies while contributing to underdevelopment elsewhere.

At its core, it’s about shifting away from an economy that benefits the elite to one that builds people’s capabilities.

As an economics professor, I’ve been restructuring my teaching based on my scholarship on critical microeconomics, critical macroeconomics and alternative ways to build the economy.

Questioning Eurocentric assumptions

This week, Delhi heard the Kanwar Yatra before seeing it.

Newspapers reported residents describing sleepless nights and rattling windows due to the ear-splitting noise. The Hindustan Times said its sound metrers clocked more than 100 decibels as trucks carrying large sound systems moved through residential areas near Kalindi Kunj and Kalkaji. Police officers directed traffic and assisted pilgrims, some drivers were asked to lower the volume, but no FIRs had been registered when the measurements were reported. In fact, in Uttar Pradesh, the Kanwar Yatra pilgrims were welcomes included flower petals showered from helicopters.

Why is noise during religious events sometimes a public health violation, but other times a celebration that the administration must accommodate?

item.title: NHPC knew of risks at Sikkim tunnel before deadly July blast, documents show
item.description: Just ten days before the tragedy, the company issued a tender for services that included management of methane gas in the tunnel.
item.content:encoded:
In the afternoon of July 20, a blast resounded through a tunnel being constructed in Sikkim’s Namchi district. Workers said that the force of the blast threw them around two metres, and that almost immediately, they could smell gas.

The explosion took place in the head-race tunnel of the 500-MW Teesta VI hydropower project being constructed by NHPC, a public enterprise. Such tunnels are the main channels that route water from a river, and lead it to turbines to generate power, before channeling the water back to the river.

The explosion occurred after a “sudden burst of suspected methane gas trapped inside the rocks which led to an explosion generating dense fumes and toxic gases”, the company said in a press release.

While some workers on site escaped the explosion, 25 others were trapped after it triggered a rockfall and blocked the tunnel’s opening. Rescue operations began immediately and concluded on the third day. There were no survivors.

The company’s press release stated that it was carrying out a “detailed investigation” to “ascertain the cause of the incident”.

But while findings of the investigation are yet to be released, company documents that Scroll has examined show that NHPC had been aware of the presence of methane on the site since at least January.

item.title: Roads in India are a deadly risk to the world’s smallest wild cat
item.description: The rusty-spotted cat is prone to being killed by vehicles due its small size, among other factors, say researchers.
item.content:encoded:
Scientists at the Wildlife Institute of India have reported two roadkill incidents of the rusty-spotted cat (Prionailurus rubiginosus) at the National Chambal Sanctuary in Etawah, Uttar Pradesh. The two records are the first documented occurrence of the small carnivore in southern Uttar Pradesh, according to the research paper published in the Journal of Threatened Taxa in May.

Roadkill data for small carnivores is heavily underreported, and these records were “a matter of chance”, according to Vishnupriya Kolipakam, a Wildlife Institute of India scientist and one of the paper’s authors.

While they add a new locality to the small cat’s known range, the wildlife sanctuary falls within its distribution range, Kolipakam said. “The wild cat has been reported from areas all around Chambal, including Kuno, Rangarh-Vishdhar, Ranthambhore, and Dholpur,” she said.

However, this follows a pattern, as seen in recent papers that have curated sighting reports of the strictly nocturnal cat. There were nine records of roadkill from the Saurashtra Peninsula in Gujarat between 2016 and 2024, and four records from Rajasthan between 2000 and 2020. In Nepal, too, where the cat was discovered as recently as 2016, there has been a record of a roadkill.

For an elusive small cat that has been rarely observed in the wild, these roadkill records add up to a significant number....

item.title: Bill criminalising insults to ‘Vande Mataram’ becomes law after President Murmu’s assent
item.description: Intentionally preventing the singing of the song or disrupting an assembly singing it can be punished with imprisonment of up to three years, the law states.
item.content:encoded:
President Droupadi Murmu on Thursday gave assent to a bill criminalising insults to the national song, Vande Mataram.

With the president’s assent, the 2026 Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Bill has become law.

The Lok Sabha passed the legislation on July 30 through a voice vote amid protests by Opposition MPs demanding a discussion on police action against youth protesters on July 20. The Rajya Sabha cleared it a day earlier.

The protests on July 20 were held against alleged mismanagement in the conduct of competitive examinations.

The law gives Vande Mataram the same statutory protection as the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana. It states that intentionally preventing the singing of the national song, or disrupting an assembly singing it can be punished with imprisonment of up to three years, a fine or both.

The 1971 Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act already makes insulting the national anthem, national flag or Constitution punishable with up to three years’ imprisonment, a fine, or both.

The legislation had faced opposition from the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam in the Lok Sabha, with MP Kanimozhi accusing the government of advancing a “Hindutva agenda” under the cover of nationalism.

Responding to the debate, Minister of State for Home Affairs Nityanand Rai said the legislation was about “Indian pride” and was not directed against any state or ideology.

The Tamil Nadu Assembly on Tuesday unanimously adopted a resolution urging the Union government to abolish the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test for undergraduate medical admissions and allow the state to admit students based on their Class 12 marks, The Hindu reported.

NEET is currently mandatory for admission to undergraduate medical courses in India.

The lone Bharatiya Janata Party MLA, M Bhojarajan, opposed the resolution and walked out before the vote.

Moving the resolution, Health Minister KG Arunraj urged the Union government to amend the 2019 National Medical Commission Act, the 2020 National Commission for Indian System of Medicine Act and the 2020 National Commission for Homoeopathy Act to enable admissions based on Class 12 results.

The resolution said that Tamil Nadu had consistently opposed NEET on grounds of social justice, equality and the rights of states in a federal system. It also said repeated question-paper leaks and other irregularities had further undermined confidence in the examination.

It also referred to the cancellation of the 2026 undergraduate medical admission exam and the subsequent re-examination, saying the developments had caused “untold mental agony” to lakhs of students and resulted in the loss of young lives.

“The examination has forfeited the trust of the students of this country,” The Hindu quoted the resolution as saying.
